name: High ankle (syndesmosis) sprain
summary: A sprain of the ligaments that bind the distal tibia and fibula, usually from external rotation and dorsiflexion of a planted foot. It recovers more slowly than a lateral sprain, and an unstable injury needs surgery.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Slower than a lateral sprain. Pooled return to play 39 days (non-surgical) and 71 days (surgical) in athletes

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based. Stable grade IIa mean 45 days, unstable grade IIb mean 64 days in 64 athletes

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No single test is accurate. Cluster palpation or dorsiflexion lunge (sensitive) with squeeze (specific, about 85%)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Weight-bearing radiographs first (clear space and overlap), then stress views or MRI if unsure

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young active adults in collision and cutting sports

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Up to 18% of ankle sprains; much less common than lateral sprains

overview:
A high ankle sprain is an injury to the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis, the ligament complex that holds the lower fibula in the notch of the tibia and keeps the ankle mortise stable. Syndesmosis injuries take longer to recover than lateral ankle sprains, and no consensus exists on optimal treatment [r1]. They are reported in up to 18% of ankle sprains, and the incidence rises in athletic activity [r2].

The key clinical decision is stable versus unstable. The ESSKA-AFAS consensus recommends classifying an acute isolated injury as stable or unstable. Stable injuries are treated non-operatively with a short-leg cast or brace, and unstable injuries are treated operatively [r3]. In a prospective series of elite athletes with grade II injuries, a positive squeeze test, concomitant deltoid injury and combined AITFL and deltoid injury separated unstable from stable injuries and predicted a longer return to sport [r4]. Most of the evidence is low level (case series, small cohorts and expert consensus), so the numbers on this page are best read as ranges, not promises [r1,r2].

epidemiology.text: A meta-analysis of 181 prospective studies found lateral sprains significantly more common than syndesmotic or medial sprains [r5]. A review gives syndesmosis injury in up to 18% of ankle sprains, rising with athletic activity [r2]. Published cohorts are mostly male athletes in collision and cutting sports. In an Australian diagnostic study, 78% of 87 participants with ankle sprain were male [r6]. High-level case series come from professional American football [r7,r8] and rugby union [r9]. Diagnostic tests for syndesmosis injury are not very specific, and time lost from sport is highly variable [r10].

intrinsic: Young, active adults: published case series enrol young, active patients [r1]
Male sex in the published sport cohorts, which probably reflects the sports played and not a biological risk [r6]
Previous lateral sprain or ankle instability (clinical reasoning; not established for syndesmosis injury)
extrinsic: Collision and cutting sports such as American football and rugby union, where a planted foot is forced into external rotation [r2,r7,r9]
Rigid, high-cuff footwear that fixes the foot (skiing and snowboarding; clinical observation)
Another player falling on the back of the leg while the foot is planted (clinical observation)

mechanism.summary: Syndesmosis injuries usually follow an external rotation mechanism [r2]. The foot is planted and the leg rotates internally on it, which is the same as the talus rotating externally in the mortise. Dorsiflexion adds to the load because the wider anterior talar dome pushes the fibula away from the tibia. The AITFL is loaded first, then the interosseous ligament and membrane, and the posterior ligament last; this order is classic cadaveric teaching and is not traced to a source on this page. A concomitant ATFL injury suggests a different, more inversion-type mechanism, and a syndesmosis that is less likely to be unstable [r4].
sequence: The athlete plants the foot, often in dorsiflexion, with the foot fixed by the ground, a boot, a ski or a tackler.
The body rotates over the planted foot, or a force rotates the leg outward on it, so the talus rotates externally inside the mortise [r2].
The talus acts like a wedge and pushes the fibula laterally and posteriorly away from the tibia, which loads the AITFL.
The AITFL stretches and then fails. As rotation continues the interosseous ligament and the interosseous membrane are loaded and fail from distal to proximal (classic teaching).

If the force continues, the posterior ligament or the deltoid ligament is injured and the clear space can widen. Deltoid injury and combined AITFL and deltoid injury were linked to instability and delayed return to sport [r4].
The athlete feels sudden pain above the ankle joint, often cannot continue and finds it hard to push off. Swelling is often modest compared with the pain.

variants.name: Contact: leg forced outward by another player
variants.description: Another player falls onto the back of the planted leg or the foot is trapped under a pile. This is a common pattern in American football and rugby [r7,r9].

variants.name: Non-contact pivot or cut
variants.description: The athlete plants and rotates the body over a fixed foot. No contact is needed.

variants.name: Combined with a lateral sprain
variants.description: An inversion sprain can injure the syndesmosis as well. A positive ATFL injury on MRI points to a different mechanism and a syndesmosis that is more often stable [r4].

variants.name: Maisonneuve pattern
variants.description: An external rotation force transmitted up the interosseous membrane fractures the proximal fibula. Proximal fibular fractures of this type are not repaired, but the syndesmosis is [r2]. Always palpate the whole fibula.

anatomy.text: The distal tibiofibular syndesmosis is a fibrous joint. It is formed by the AITFL at the front, the interosseous ligament and the interosseous membrane between the bones, and the posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (PITFL) behind. Together they hold the fibula in the tibial notch (incisura) and let it move slightly with ankle motion. They keep the lateral wall of the mortise tight around the talus, which is wider at the front and so presses the fibula outward in dorsiflexion. On a radiograph, stability is judged by the tibiofibular clear space and overlap and the medial clear space [r3,r11]. The deltoid ligament on the medial side adds to mortise stability, which is why deltoid injury changes the prognosis [r4].

structures.name: Anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL)
structures.role: The strongest anterior restraint to fibular external rotation and lateral displacement. It is the ligament most often palpated and the first to be injured.

structures.name: Interosseous ligament and membrane
structures.role: Hold the shafts of the tibia and fibula together and spread load up the leg. Failure here lets the clear space widen.

structures.name: Posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (PITFL)
structures.role: The deep, strong posterior restraint. It is usually injured only with higher-energy injuries.

structures.name: Deltoid ligament
structures.role: Medial stabiliser of the talus. Combined AITFL and deltoid injury delayed return to sport and was linked to instability [r4].

structures.name: Tibiofibular clear space and overlap
structures.role: Radiographic measures of syndesmosis integrity on the AP and mortise views [r3,r11].

structures.name: Talus and mortise
structures.role: The talus is wider anteriorly, so dorsiflexion pushes the fibula laterally and rotation loads the syndesmosis.

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Ligament collagen fails in tension once the rotation and dorsiflexion load exceeds its capacity. A mild injury is a stretch or microtear of the AITFL with an intact syndesmosis. A moderate injury involves a partial or complete AITFL tear with the interosseous ligament at least partly torn. A severe injury disrupts the AITFL, the interosseous ligament and often the PITFL or deltoid, so the fibula can move away from the tibia under load [r3,r4].

The syndesmosis cannot rest as the lateral ligaments can: it is loaded with every step because the talus moves in the mortise on weight-bearing and dorsiflexion. This is the main reason it recovers more slowly than a lateral sprain [r1]. Pain is often out of proportion to the apparent injury [r6]. The extent of injury on MRI does not predict recovery well: in 17 professional football players, the width of syndesmotic separation correlated with time lost, but individual ligament injury and the proximal extent of oedema did not [r8].

structures.name: AITFL
structures.effect: Stretch, partial tear or rupture. It is the ligament most often injured.

structures.name: Interosseous ligament and membrane
structures.effect: Injured when rotation continues. Disruption lets the fibula separate from the tibia.

structures.name: PITFL
structures.effect: Injured in more severe injuries; it is the last of the syndesmotic ligaments to fail (classic teaching).

structures.name: Deltoid ligament
structures.effect: Often injured with the syndesmosis. It was associated with a higher chance of instability and longer return to sport [r4].

structures.name: Talar dome and tibial plafond cartilage
structures.effect: Can be bruised or damaged as the talus rotates. Osteochondral injury is a recognised cause of persistent pain (clinical reasoning).

structures.name: Fibula (Maisonneuve)
structures.effect: An external rotation force can fracture the proximal fibula and leave the syndesmosis unstable [r2].

muscles.name: Peroneals and tibialis posterior
muscles.effect: Guard the painful ankle and are weak and slow to react afterwards (clinical reasoning).

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius and soleus
muscles.effect: Disuse and pain reduce calf capacity. Rising onto the toes loads the syndesmosis, so calf work needs careful grading.

muscles.name: Tibialis anterior
muscles.effect: Reduced dorsiflexor control alters foot position at heel strike (clinical reasoning).

muscles.name: Hip and quadriceps muscles
muscles.effect: Lose strength in a boot or with protected weight-bearing. They are retrained in the first stage.

cellular.description: Torn vessels bleed and a fibrin clot forms. Platelets, neutrophils and macrophages clear debris and release growth factors. Pain and swelling peak.
Fibroblasts lay down disorganised type III collagen and new capillaries grow. The ligament is weak and tolerates only graded load.
Type III collagen is replaced by aligned type I collagen along the line of load. The scar matures slowly and is weaker than normal ligament for months (general ligament biology).

systems.effect: Pain and loss of afferent input from ligament mechanoreceptors reduce balance and protective control. Protective guarding also changes gait.
Bleeding and inflammation cause pain and swelling over the anterolateral ankle, usually with less visible bruising than a lateral sprain.
Antalgic gait and a boot shift load to the other leg, knee and hip, and quadriceps and gluteal strength fall (clinical reasoning).
Fear of re-injury is common because push-off and pivoting are painful for weeks. The athlete may also be frustrated by a longer recovery than they expected from a sprain [r1].
An unrecognised unstable syndesmosis can cause chronic pain and instability, and in the chronic stage the evidence for treatment is limited to case series [r12].

grading.system: Stable versus unstable (ESSKA-AFAS), with Calder's subdivision of grade II

grades.description: Stretch or partial tear of the AITFL only. The syndesmosis is intact on stress testing and on weight-bearing radiographs. This is a conventional description, and there is no validated grading system [r1,r3].
grades.prognosis: Usually the shortest recovery. Stable injuries are treated non-operatively with a short-leg cast or brace [r3].

grades.description: Partial or complete AITFL injury with the interosseous ligament involved but no dynamic instability on arthroscopy. Treated with a boot and rehabilitation [r4].
grades.prognosis: Mean return to sport 45 days (range 23–63) in 28 athletes [r4].

grades.description: Clinically unstable and confirmed unstable at arthroscopy, with the syndesmosis then stabilised. A positive squeeze test and deltoid injury made instability more likely [r4].
grades.prognosis: Mean return to sport 64 days (range 27–104) in the same series [r4].

grades.description: Disruption of the syndesmotic ligaments with a widened clear space or mortise on weight-bearing or stress imaging, often with deltoid injury or a fibular fracture [r2,r3].
grades.prognosis: Operative stabilisation is the standard treatment for unstable injuries [r3]. Pooled return to play after surgery was 71 days, versus 39 days after non-surgical care, but the groups differ in severity [r13].

timeframes.summary: Syndesmosis injuries recover more slowly than lateral sprains [r1]. In a meta-analysis of 1133 syndesmotic sprains in athletes, mean return to play was 52 days, 39 days after non-surgical care and 71 days after surgery [r13]. Individual time lost varies widely, from 0 to 137 days in older case series [r1]. Time is a guide; criteria decide.

healing.description: Bleeding, swelling and pain peak. A boot or brace and protected weight-bearing are common for stable injuries [r7].
Disorganised collagen and new capillaries. Graded weight-bearing, range and early strength work.
Collagen realigns along the line of load. Running, then cutting and pivoting are rebuilt.
Slow maturation of the scar. Persisting pain or instability at this stage should be re-imaged.

milestones.label: Weight-bearing without a boot
milestones.note: Typical for stable injuries after a brief period of protected weight-bearing (clinical convention) [r7]

milestones.label: Jogging in a straight line
milestones.note: Needs pain-free hopping and no clear-space pain (clinical convention)

milestones.label: Return to sport, stable grade IIa (mean)
Return to sport, unstable grade IIb (mean)
Pooled mean return to play, all treatments

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based. In athletes, pooled return to play was 99% at a mean of 52 days (39 days non-surgical, 71 days surgical) [r13]. A clinical review of professional American football players describes 2–6 weeks for stable injuries [r7]. Unstable injuries need longer. These are ranges from case series, and the surgical and non-surgical groups differ in severity.

symptoms: Sudden pain above the ankle joint and at the front of the lower leg after a twist, often with the foot trapped
Pain on push-off, running, stairs and rising onto the toes, and often a feeling that the ankle will not trust load
Pain on dorsiflexion and external rotation, for example turning on a planted foot
Pain out of proportion to the visible swelling or bruising [r6]
Difficulty or inability to hop on the injured leg [r6]
signs: Tenderness over the AITFL and the anterior syndesmosis, the most sensitive clinical test (92%) against MRI in one study [r6]
Pain with the squeeze test, the external rotation stress test or the dorsiflexion–external rotation stress test [r6,r14]
Mild swelling and less lateral bruising than after a lateral sprain, with possible medial tenderness over the deltoid
Restricted weight-bearing dorsiflexion with pain at the front of the lower ankle [r14]
Antalgic gait with a shortened push-off and inability to single-leg hop [r6]

subjective: Mechanism: planted foot, external rotation, dorsiflexion, a tackler or a trapped foot, versus a clear inversion roll [r2]
Where the pain is: above the joint line and anterior (syndesmosis), lateral (ATFL and CFL), medial (deltoid) or along the proximal fibula (Maisonneuve)
Ability to weight-bear and to hop, and whether pain seems out of proportion to the injury [r6]
Sound, sensation or a feeling of the ankle 'opening' at the time
Sport, level, position, footwear and the calendar of the season, because the decision between surgery and rehabilitation affects the timeline
Previous ankle injuries and giving way
Neurovascular symptoms: numbness, pins and needles, a cold or pale foot
observation: Swelling over the anterior ankle and distal tibiofibular area
Bruising (often less than a lateral sprain) and its spread
Weight-bearing posture and hindfoot alignment compared with the other side
palpation: AITFL and the anterior syndesmosis, with tenderness extending proximally along the interosseous membrane
Entire fibula down to the head to exclude a Maisonneuve fracture [r2]
Medial malleolus and the deltoid ligament; medial tenderness raises the chance of instability [r4]
ATFL, CFL and the peroneal tendons, to separate a lateral component
Bone first by the Ottawa rules: posterior edge and tip of both malleoli, base of the fifth metatarsal and navicular [r15]
rangeOfMotion: Active and passive dorsiflexion, plantarflexion and inversion and eversion, compared with the other side
Weight-bearing dorsiflexion lunge: pain at the front of the ankle in the lunge was a sensitive finding, with the dorsiflexion lunge reaching 75% sensitivity in a pooled analysis [r14]
strength: Calf raise capacity once weight-bearing is allowed; single-leg raises load the syndesmosis
Peroneal, tibialis posterior and tibialis anterior strength as pain permits
Hip abductor and extensor strength, because a boot reduces proximal loading (clinical reasoning)
neuro: Sensation over the dorsum and lateral foot (superficial peroneal and sural nerves)
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses and capillary refill, particularly with marked swelling
functional: Single-leg hop: inability to hop had 89% sensitivity for syndesmosis injury in one diagnostic study [r6]
Single-leg stance and single-leg heel raise
Straight-line jog, then cutting and pivot drills when pain and swelling allow
Weight-bearing dorsiflexion lunge comparison with the other side

specialTests.name: Syndesmosis ligament palpation (AITFL and interosseous membrane)
specialTests.purpose: Screen for syndesmosis injury; the most sensitive clinical test in the studies read
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the AITFL anterior to the distal tibiofibular joint, then follow the interosseous membrane proximally. Compare with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Focal tenderness over the AITFL or along the interosseous membrane
specialTests.sensitivity: 92% (95% CI 79–98) in a pooled analysis; 92% in one MRI-referenced study (87 participants)

specialTests.name: Squeeze test
specialTests.purpose: Raise suspicion of syndesmosis injury and of instability. An earlier review found conflicting results for the squeeze test across two accuracy studies [r16].
specialTests.procedure: Compress the tibia and fibula together at mid-calf, about half-way up the leg. Note where pain is felt.
specialTests.positive: Pain at the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis, not pain at the site of compression
specialTests.specificity: 85% (95% CI 81–89) pooled across 4 studies; 88% in the 87-participant study
specialTests.lrPositive: 2.15 (95% CI 0.86–5.39) in the 87-participant study. A positive squeeze test made instability 9.5 times as likely in grade II athletes [r4].

specialTests.name: External rotation (Kleiger) stress test
specialTests.purpose: Reproduce the injury mechanism and test the syndesmosis under rotation
specialTests.procedure: Seated, with the knee flexed to 90° and the ankle in neutral or dorsiflexion, stabilise the leg and externally rotate the foot. The dorsiflexion–external rotation variant adds dorsiflexion.
specialTests.positive: Pain over the anterior syndesmosis (not the medial ankle alone)
specialTests.sensitivity: 71% for the dorsiflexion–external rotation stress test (87 participants)
specialTests.specificity: 78% (95% CI 73–82) pooled for external rotation (4 studies)
specialTests.lrNegative: 0.46 (95% CI 0.27–0.79) for the dorsiflexion–external rotation test

specialTests.name: Dorsiflexion lunge (with compression) test
specialTests.purpose: Weight-bearing screen for anterior tibiofibular pain
specialTests.procedure: In a knee-to-wall lunge, ask about anterior ankle pain. In the compression version the examiner squeezes the tibia and fibula together at the ankle during the lunge.
specialTests.positive: Pain at the anterior syndesmosis, or reduced lunge distance compared with the other side

specialTests.name: Cotton and fibular translation tests
specialTests.purpose: Test for increased fibular or talar translation in the mortise. The ESSKA-AFAS panel recommends them with AITFL palpation [r3].
specialTests.procedure: Cotton test: with the tibia fixed, translate the talus laterally. Fibular translation test: translate the fibula anteroposteriorly relative to the tibia. Compare with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Increased translation or pain, or a soft end-feel, compared with the other side

specialTests.name: Single-leg hop and pain out of proportion
specialTests.purpose: Clinical features that add to the cluster of syndesmosis signs
specialTests.procedure: Ask the patient to hop on the injured leg. Record whether pain appears out of proportion to the apparent injury.
specialTests.positive: Inability to hop; pain out of proportion to swelling or bruising

clinicalRules.name: Ottawa ankle rules (exclude fracture first)
clinicalRules.description: Request radiographs if there is pain near the malleoli with bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to take four steps. In a meta-analysis of 66 studies, the ankle rules had pooled sensitivity of 99.4% (95% CI 97.9–99.8) and specificity of 35.3% (95% CI 28.8–42.3), so they are good for ruling out fracture [r15].

clinicalRules.name: Test cluster for syndesmosis injury
clinicalRules.description: No individual test has both high sensitivity and high specificity [r14,r16]. A reasonable approach is to start with sensitive findings (palpation, dorsiflexion lunge, inability to hop) and then add specific findings (squeeze test, pain out of proportion). The authors of the pooled analysis note that the tests cannot separate stable from unstable injuries, so management decisions need imaging or arthroscopy [r14].

outcomeMeasures.name: Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM)
outcomeMeasures.use: Self-reported function in daily life and sport, tracked at each stage

outcomeMeasures.name: Lower Extremity Functional Scale (LEFS)
outcomeMeasures.use: General lower-limb function, easy to repeat at every visit

outcomeMeasures.name: Single-leg hop for distance and single-leg heel raise to fatigue
outcomeMeasures.use: Performance measures for load and push-off capacity; compare limb symmetry

outcomeMeasures.name: Weight-bearing dorsiflexion lunge distance
outcomeMeasures.use: Tracks dorsiflexion range and anterior ankle pain

outcomeMeasures.name: Pain at squeeze and external rotation tests
outcomeMeasures.use: Repeat the tests at each visit; persisting pain suggests ongoing syndesmotic irritability

imaging.indication: Every suspected syndesmosis injury, and Ottawa-positive injuries. Radiographs under the physiological stress of weight-bearing are recommended [r2].
imaging.findings: Tibiofibular clear space, tibiofibular overlap and medial clear space [r3,r11]. In a retrospective series of 79 patients, proposed intact-syndesmosis values were clear space under about 4.6 mm (men) or 4.3 mm (women), measured 1 cm above the plafond [r11]. A common surgical indication is widening over 2 mm on radiograph [r17].

imaging.modality: Stress radiograph (external rotation) or comparison weight-bearing views
imaging.indication: When initial radiographs are normal but instability is suspected
imaging.findings: Dynamic widening of the clear space or medial clear space. If images are inconclusive, external rotation stress testing or MRI is advised [r2].

imaging.indication: Persisting pain, an uncertain diagnosis or a decision about surgery. It can confirm the diagnosis or show alternative injuries [r8].
imaging.findings: AITFL, interosseous membrane, PITFL and deltoid injury; bone marrow oedema and osteochondral injury. In professional football players, agreement between radiologists was almost perfect for syndesmotic membrane injury but only fair for the AITFL [r8]. Syndesmotic separation width correlated with time lost, but the extent of injury did not [r8].

imaging.indication: A clinically unstable grade II injury, where it confirms dynamic instability and guides stabilisation [r4]
imaging.findings: Widening of the distal tibiofibular joint on arthroscopic assessment [r17]

differentials.name: Lateral ankle sprain
differentials.distinguishing: Inversion mechanism, lateral swelling and bruising, tenderness over the ATFL and CFL, negative squeeze test. It often coexists with a syndesmosis injury.

differentials.name: Medial ankle (deltoid) sprain
differentials.distinguishing: Eversion or external rotation mechanism with medial tenderness. The deltoid is often injured with the syndesmosis.

differentials.name: Ankle (malleolar) fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Bone tenderness at the malleoli, inability to take four steps, deformity or a widened mortise on radiograph. A fibular fracture above the syndesmosis implies syndesmosis disruption.

differentials.name: Osteochondral lesion of the talus
differentials.distinguishing: Deep ankle pain, catching or effusion that persists beyond 6 weeks; MRI confirms. It can coexist.

differentials.name: Chronic ankle instability
differentials.distinguishing: Recurrent giving way more than 12 months after a lateral sprain, with lateral laxity. Chronic syndesmotic instability gives anterior pain and a feeling of looseness.

differentials.name: Anterior ankle impingement
differentials.distinguishing: Anterior pain at end-range dorsiflexion with a palpable osteophyte; no rotational mechanism

differentials.name: Peroneal tendon subluxation or tear
differentials.distinguishing: Retromalleolar pain and snapping on resisted eversion; tenderness behind the lateral malleolus

differentials.name: Fifth metatarsal base fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal after an inversion injury

redFlags: Positive Ottawa ankle rules, inability to take four steps, deformity or bony tenderness: arrange radiographs the same day to exclude fracture or dislocation [r15].
Tenderness along the proximal fibula, severe medial and lateral pain, or a widened mortise: suspect a Maisonneuve fracture or an unstable injury and arrange urgent orthopaedic review [r2,r3].
Widening of the clear space on weight-bearing or stress views, or a clinically unstable test cluster: refer for orthopaedic assessment, because an unstable injury is managed operatively [r3,r4].
Absent pulses, a cold or pale foot, severe swelling with pain on passive toe stretch, or progressive numbness: suspect neurovascular compromise or compartment syndrome and send to emergency.
Calf pain, swelling or breathlessness, especially in a boot or cast: consider deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism (clinical reasoning).

Pain, swelling or giving way at about 6 weeks without improvement (a clinical convention): re-image with weight-bearing radiographs and MRI for chronic instability, osteochondral lesion or occult fracture.

management.principles: Management follows the stable-versus-unstable decision [r3]. Stable injuries are treated non-operatively with a short period of protection (a boot, brace or short-leg cast), then progressive loading and a graded return to running, cutting and pivoting [r3,r7]. Unstable injuries, shown by a widened clear space, a positive stress test or arthroscopic instability, are treated surgically [r3,r4]. Physiotherapists need to recognise the injury early, because an unstable syndesmosis treated as a lateral sprain risks persistent pain and instability [r1,r2]. There are no randomised trials of rehabilitation for syndesmosis sprains. The programme below is built from case series, a clinical review and the general ankle sprain guideline, which prefers supervised exercise to passive modalities for ankle sprains in general [r7,r18]. Decisions should be shared with the athlete, the surgeon and the team.

medical.name: Short-leg cast, boot or brace with protected weight-bearing for stable injuries
medical.description: The ESSKA-AFAS consensus recommends non-operative treatment with a short-leg cast or brace for stable injuries [r3]. A clinical review of professional football players describes a brief period of immobilisation and protected weight-bearing, followed by progressive strengthening and running [r7]. The exact length of immobilisation is not standardised.

medical.name: Surgical stabilisation of unstable injuries
medical.description: Unstable injuries should be managed operatively [r3]. In a prospective series, athletes with arthroscopically confirmed instability (grade IIb) had the syndesmosis stabilised and returned at a mean of 64 days [r4]. A survey of 742 providers found suture-button (flexible) fixation preferred by 47.1%, and considerable variability in the time to weight-bearing, running and full participation [r17]. A common indication was widening over 2 mm on radiograph [r17]. The evidence base is mostly case series and consensus.

medical.name: Surgery for chronic syndesmotic instability
medical.description: In a systematic review of 15 case series on chronic injuries (over 6 months), pooled success was 87.9% for screw fixation, 79.4% for arthrodesis and 78.7% for arthroscopic debridement. Evidence is limited to case series, so these figures are not comparative [r12].

medical.name: Platelet-rich plasma injection into the AITFL
medical.description: The only study found was a pilot of 10 rugby players given a single ultrasound-guided PRP injection, compared with 11 historical controls. Return to play was faster in the PRP group (p = 0.048), but the authors describe it as a feasibility pilot [r9]. It cannot support routine use.

physio.name: Progressive loading and graded return to running
physio.description: After a short period of protection, progress weight-bearing, range, strength and then running by criteria. The clinical review describes progressive strengthening exercises and running after brief immobilisation [r7]. Load calf work and dorsiflexion gradually, because both stress the syndesmosis.

physio.name: Test-cluster diagnosis and early referral of suspected instability
physio.description: Physiotherapists screen with sensitive then specific tests [r14,r6], order or request weight-bearing imaging, and refer when the cluster is positive or the athlete does not progress. Clinical examination alone cannot reliably separate stable from unstable injuries [r14].

physio.name: Sensorimotor and balance training
physio.description: Single-leg balance, perturbation and landing control are standard parts of ankle rehabilitation, and the general ankle sprain guideline prefers supervised exercise-based programmes to passive modalities [r18]. There are no syndesmosis-specific trials.

physio.name: Manual therapy and taping
physio.description: No syndesmosis-specific evidence was found. Tape or a brace may add comfort and confidence during return to running (clinical convention). Avoid manual techniques that stress the syndesmosis into external rotation while it is healing.

physio.name: Return to sport before the syndesmosis is stable
physio.description: Pivoting and cutting before pain, swelling and dynamic stability have settled risks chronic syndesmotic pain and instability [r1,r12]. Time from injury alone is a poor guide, because return-to-play times ranged from 0 to 137 days in case series [r1].

education: A high ankle sprain is a different injury from a rolled ankle. It takes longer to heal, and sometimes needs surgery.
Protect the ankle early, but start moving as soon as your physio and doctor agree. The injury is slow because the ligaments are loaded with every step.
Expect a recovery measured in weeks to months, not days. For stable injuries in athletes, return to play is roughly 6 weeks on average, but it varies widely [r4,r13].
Pivoting and sudden turns are the last things to return. Rushing them is the most common reason for setbacks.
Tell your physio if pain persists beyond about 6 weeks, or if the ankle feels loose, because it needs imaging and perhaps a surgeon.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and conservative with the rotational loads. The programme is for a stable injury treated non-operatively. Unstable injuries treated surgically need the surgeon's protocol, which differs in weight-bearing and timing [r17]. No validated return-to-sport criteria exist for syndesmosis injury. Time frames are ranges from case series and a clinical review [r4,r7], dosages are common clinical conventions and not trial doses, and the exercises exist to restore range, load capacity and control without stressing the syndesmosis in external rotation.

stages.name: Protect and settle
goals: Protect the syndesmosis with a boot or brace as advised
Keep hips, knee and the other leg strong
precautions: Exclude fracture, Maisonneuve injury and an unstable injury first (red flags)
Avoid external rotation and forced dorsiflexion
Follow the weight-bearing instructions of the medical team
Watch for DVT symptoms in a boot or cast

exercises.name: Ankle alphabet (pain-free range)
exercises.cues: Move from the ankle, small and smooth

exercises.name: Isometric dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, inversion and eversion
exercises.dosage: 5 × 10 s at low effort, 2–3 times daily
exercises.cues: Press into the wall or your hand without moving the ankle

exercises.name: Quadriceps and hip strengthening that avoids the ankle
Gentle weight-bearing in the boot as allowed
exercises.dosage: Short, frequent walks, increasing daily as pain allows
exercises.cues: Heel strike, roll through, no limp

progressionCriteria: Walking without a limp in the boot or brace

stages.name: Restore range and basic load
goals: Walk without a boot with a normal heel–toe gait
Keep the ankle comfortable the day after exercise
precautions: Progress dorsiflexion and calf work gradually and stop if front-of-ankle pain returns
No twisting or pivoting on the foot
Keep tape or brace if it reduces pain

exercises.name: Weight-bearing dorsiflexion lunge (knee-to-wall)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10 holds of 5 s, daily, within comfortable range
exercises.cues: Heel down, knee over the second toe, stop at first pinch

exercises.name: Band-resisted ankle exercises (all four directions)
exercises.cues: Move only the ankle, no leg rotation

exercises.name: Double-leg calf raise
exercises.cues: Rise evenly over both big toes

exercises.name: Single-leg balance
exercises.dosage: 3 × 20–30 s, near a support, progressing to eyes closed
exercises.cues: Soft knee, stay tall, keep the foot pointing straight ahead

progressionCriteria: Walking 20 minutes without a boot and without a limp
Dorsiflexion lunge within a few millimetres of the other side without anterior pain

stages.name: Strength, control and running
precautions: Introduce running in straight lines first
No cutting, pivoting or twisting until criteria are met
Stop and re-assess if pain, giving way or swelling returns

exercises.name: Single-leg calf raise (progress from double-leg, then add load)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–12, then add a dumbbell, 3 times per week
exercises.cues: Slow lowering over 3 s, rise over the big toe

exercises.name: Step-ups and controlled step-downs
exercises.cues: Knee over the second toe, control the lowering

exercises.name: Single-leg squat to a chair
exercises.cues: Level pelvis, foot straight, no rotation

exercises.name: Walk–jog progression
exercises.dosage: 1 min jog, 1 min walk, 8–10 rounds, building jog time every 2–3 sessions
exercises.cues: Short, quiet steps under the body

exercises.name: Double-leg landing, then single-leg hop and stick
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8 double-leg landings, then 3 × 5 single-leg hops with a 2 s stick
exercises.cues: Soft landing, ankle, knee and hip bend together

progressionCriteria: Jogging 20 minutes without pain or swelling
Single-leg calf raise 15 repetitions or more, close to the other side (clinical convention)
No pain on the squeeze test or the external rotation stress test

stages.name: Cutting, pivoting and return to sport
goals: Controlled change of direction and pivoting
precautions: Introduce rotation gradually: planned before reactive, slow before fast
No unrestricted play until criteria are met
Keep tape or a brace if it improves confidence
Re-image if pain persists or instability is suspected

exercises.name: Planned cutting and change-of-direction drills
exercises.dosage: 2–3 sessions per week, progressing angle and speed
exercises.cues: Plant the foot under the knee and keep it pointing the way you move

exercises.name: Controlled pivot drills (slow to fast)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 6 each way, 2–3 times per week, starting at 50% effort
exercises.cues: Turn the whole body over the foot, no twisting inside the shoe

exercises.name: Lateral bounds and hop-and-stick
exercises.cues: Land on the full foot, stay quiet at the ankle

exercises.name: Sport-specific drills with contact build-up
exercises.dosage: Graded exposure within team training, starting at about 50% volume
exercises.cues: Land and turn with hips and knees bent

exercises.name: Weighted single-leg calf raise and balance maintenance
exercises.dosage: 10–15 minutes before training, 2–3 times per week

progressionCriteria: Full pain-free range, no swelling after full training
Hop tests within about 90% of the other leg (clinical convention)
Squeeze and external rotation stress tests pain-free
Confidence rated high and clearance from the surgeon or sports physician where one is involved

criteria: No validated return-to-sport criteria exist for syndesmosis injury. These are common clinical conventions.
No pain at rest or after a full training session, and no swelling
Squeeze test and external rotation stress test pain-free
Full, symmetrical weight-bearing dorsiflexion and a normal gait, walk and jog
Single-leg hop and calf-raise capacity around 90% of the other leg (clinical convention)
Cutting, pivoting and landing without pain, giving way or compensation
For unstable injuries, clearance from the surgeon and follow-up imaging showing the clear space is maintained
tests: Single, triple and side hop tests
Squeeze test and external rotation stress test
Planned then reactive change-of-direction and pivot drills

prognosis: Most athletes return to sport. In a meta-analysis of 18 articles and 1133 syndesmotic sprains, the overall return to play was 99% (95% CI 96–100%), the mean was 52 days (95% CI 39–66), and a low incidence of recurrence and complications was reported [r13]. Time lost is wide-ranging: older case series reported 0–137 days [r1]. In a prospective series of 64 professional athletes, all returned to the same level, after a mean of 45 days for stable and 64 days for unstable injuries [r4]. Outcomes are less certain in the general population. In the older case series reviewed, one reported acceptable outcomes in only 44% of patients while two others rated outcomes good to excellent, and the studies used no consistent diagnosis, grading or treatment protocols [r1]. Missed instability can lead to chronic pain, and the treatment of chronic injury rests on case series [r12].
prevention: There are no proven prevention programmes specific to syndesmosis injury. The general ankle sprain guideline recommends supervised exercise and considers braces for preventing recurrent lateral sprains, which are not syndesmosis-specific [r18].
Complete rehabilitation of any ankle sprain, including dorsiflexion range, calf capacity and balance, before returning to sport (clinical convention).
Recognise and manage syndesmosis injuries early rather than as 'a slow lateral sprain' [r1,r2].
Teach pivoting and cutting technique with the foot and knee aligned, and manage footwear that fixes the foot (clinical convention).
clinicalPearls: If a sprain is slow and the pain is above the joint line, do a squeeze test, an external rotation test and a hop test before you call it a lateral sprain [r6,r14].
No single test works. Start with sensitive findings (palpation 92%, hop inability 89%, dorsiflexion lunge 75%) and add specific ones (squeeze about 85%, pain out of proportion) [r6,r14].
A positive squeeze test, medial tenderness or deltoid injury raise the chance of an unstable injury and a longer return to sport [r4].
Palpate the whole fibula to the head. A proximal fibular fracture means the syndesmosis is probably unstable (Maisonneuve) [r2].
Take weight-bearing radiographs: normal non-weight-bearing films can hide instability [r2,r3].
Be honest about the evidence: treatment studies are case series, time lost ranged from 0 to 137 days in older case series, and 'about 6 weeks' is an average, not a plan [r1,r13].

animation.title: How a high ankle sprain happens

forces.label: Leg rotates outward on the planted foot

captions.text: A footballer cuts hard on the right foot.
The foot plants firmly in the turf, with the ankle dorsiflexed.
The body keeps rotating over the planted foot, or a tackler forces the leg outward.
External rotation and dorsiflexion push the talus against the fibula.
The ligaments between the tibia and fibula are overloaded, and the ankle gives.
Pain above the ankle joint ends the play.
Zooming into the right ankle.

actions.text: AITFL: holds the fibula to the tibia

actions.label: Talus rotates out and pushes the fibula away

captions.text: The AITFL runs from the tibia to the front of the fibula and holds the two bones together.
External rotation turns the talus in the mortise and pushes the fibula laterally.
The AITFL stretches and tears, usually the first ligament to fail.
If rotation continues, the interosseous ligament is loaded and fails.
The fibula can separate from the tibia, and the clear space widens. This is an unstable injury.
The deltoid ligament is often injured too, which makes instability more likely.
Pain sits above the joint line. These ligaments are loaded with every step, so they heal slowly.
Healthy ligament: crimped type I collagen fibres aligned along the line of load.
Under rotation the crimp straightens and the fibres stretch.
Beyond the elastic range, fibrils slide and begin to fail.
Fibre failure ends in a partial or complete tear of the AITFL.
Torn vessels bleed and the clot forms a scaffold for repair.
Inflammation: neutrophils, then macrophages, clear debris over the first few days.
Fibroblasts lay down disorganised type III collagen and new capillaries.
Collagen realigns along the line of load. The scar stays weaker than normal ligament for months.
